title: Give Us a King
summary: When Samuel grows old, his sons, whom he has appointed as judges, take bribes and pervert justice. The elders of Israel come to Samuel at Ramah and demand a king to judge them like all the other nations. Samuel is displeased and prays; the LORD tells him to listen to the people, since they have rejected not Samuel but God himself as their king, but to warn them what a king will do. Samuel describes a king who will take their sons, daughters, fields, and harvests, but the people insist, and the LORD tells Samuel to give them a king.
story: Chapter 7 closed with Samuel judging Israel faithfully and the LORD giving victory over the Philistines. Now, a generation later, the pattern breaks down in a way the reader has seen before. Eli's sons were corrupt priests; Samuel's sons are corrupt judges. The elders' demand for a king is the hinge of the whole book. Everything before it has been the last chapter of the age of the judges; everything after it concerns the kings. Judges ended with the refrain that there was no king in Israel, and many readers took that as a longing for one. Chapter 8 complicates that hope. A king may bring order, but the reason Israel asks, and the kind of king it wants, is a problem.
historical:
The request comes near the end of the eleventh century BC, when Israel faced mounting pressure from the Philistines in the west and, as chapter 11 will show, the Ammonites in the east. Surrounding peoples, including the Philistines, the Ammonites, the Moabites, and the Edomites, had kings or strong rulers who could organize armies. A tribal federation led by occasional judges must have seemed weak by comparison, and the elders' stated reason is precisely military: a king to go out before us and fight our battles.

Samuel's warning describes the standard practices of ancient Near Eastern monarchy: conscription for chariot corps and royal service, forced labor on royal lands, taxation of a tenth of the harvest, confiscation of property for royal officials. Scholars have compared this description with royal administrative texts from the Canaanite city of Ugarit and elsewhere in the region, and it fits the kind of kingship that existed in Canaan during the late second millennium BC. Some scholars think the speech was shaped by later experience of Solomon's heavy demands (1 Kings 4-5; 12:4), while others see it as a realistic warning based on the kingdoms Israel already knew.
cultural:
Kingship in the ancient Near East was not only a political office but a religious one. Kings were commonly understood as chosen by the gods, sometimes as divine sons, and they served as the chief link between the gods and the people. Israel's law had anticipated a request for a king and laid down limits: he must be chosen by God, must not multiply horses, wives, or wealth, and must read and obey the law (Deuteronomy 17:14-20). That law begins by imagining the people saying they want a king like all the nations around them, almost the exact words of the elders here.

The elders who approach Samuel represented the tribes and clans and held real authority in local and national decisions. Beersheba, where Samuel's sons judged, was the southern limit of Israelite settlement, far from Samuel's home at Ramah. Taking bribes and perverting justice directly violated the law of Deuteronomy 16:19, which forbade judges to accept a bribe because it blinds the eyes of the wise.
literary: The chapter is built almost entirely of speeches, framed by the elders' demand and the LORD's permission. The key word is the Hebrew verb shama, to listen or obey. The LORD tells Samuel three times to listen to the people's voice (verses 7, 9, and 22), and the people refuse to listen to Samuel (verse 19). Samuel's warning speech is organized around the verb take, used four times in verses 11-16 and implied throughout, and it ends with the stark conclusion that the people will become slaves (verse 17). The speech also plays on the word mishpat, which means justice or judgment in verse 3 but is translated manner or custom in verses 9 and 11: Israel wanted a king to give them justice, and Samuel describes the king's mishpat as taking. The narrator's sympathies are clear but restrained, and the LORD's response holds judgment and grace together: the request is a rejection of God, and he grants it anyway.

outline.t: The elders demand a king like the nations
The LORD: they have rejected Me; warn them
The manner of the king: he will take
The people insist, and the LORD grants their request

doctrines.note: The chapter assumes that the LORD is Israel's true king. The demand for a human king like the nations is a rejection of his rule. Yet God does not abandon them; he will give a king and later make the throne of David a vehicle of his own kingdom. The question the rest of Scripture pursues is what it looks like for a human king to rule under the kingship of God.

The LORD places the request in a long pattern of forsaking him and serving other gods since the exodus. The desire to be like the nations and to trust in a king who fights their battles is a form of misplaced trust, putting confidence in human power rather than in God.

God grants a request he disapproves of and works through it. The chapter shows that God can let people have what they ask for as a form of judgment, while still weaving their choices into his purposes.

words.note: Melekh, king, appearing nine times in this chapter. In the ancient Near East the word covered rulers from great emperors to kings of small city-states. The chapter's tension is between two kinds of kingship: the LORD's rule over Israel and the human kingship the people want.

Ma'as, to reject or despise. God tells Samuel that the people have not rejected him but have rejected God as their king. The same verb returns when God rejects Saul for rejecting his word (15:23, 26). The book is built on these reversals of rejection.

Mishpat, which can mean justice, judgment, legal decision, or custom and manner. Samuel's sons perverted mishpat (justice), and Samuel describes the mishpat (manner) of the king. The play on the word suggests that the king who is supposed to bring justice will bring his own kind of order, much of it taking.

Shama, to hear, listen, or obey. The chapter repeats it often. God tells Samuel to listen to the people, the people refuse to listen to Samuel, and Samuel repeats their words in the LORD's hearing. Whether Israel and its king will listen to God becomes the test of the monarchy.

christ: The chapter asks what kind of king God's people need. Israel wanted a king to fight their battles and make them like the nations. The Bible's later story shows a long line of kings who mostly confirmed Samuel's warning, taking rather than giving. The Gospels present Jesus as the king whose kingdom reverses Samuel's description: he came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), and he warned his disciples that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it must not be so among them (Mark 10:42-43). The link is thematic. First Samuel 8 does not predict Jesus, but its portrait of the king who takes throws into relief the one the New Testament calls the true King, who gives.

hard.q: If Deuteronomy 17 allows Israel to have a king, why is asking for one treated as a rejection of God?
hard.a: The chapter seems to condemn what the Law permits, and interpreters have explained the tension in several ways. One view focuses on motive and timing: the problem is not kingship itself but a demand to be like the nations and a lack of trust in God's deliverance, made while God was actively leading through Samuel. Deuteronomy 17 required that the king be one the LORD chooses; the elders ask Samuel to appoint one on their terms. A second view notes that God had promised kings in Israel's future (Genesis 17:6; 35:11; 49:10) and sees the fault in grasping for kingship before God's time and chosen king, David. A third, common among critical scholars, sees Samuel as combining sources with different attitudes to the monarchy, some favorable and some hostile, and reads the chapter as an honest record of Israel's mixed experience of its kings. Across these views, the text is clear that the request came from a failure to trust God as king, and equally clear that God took up the institution anyway.

questions: Israel wanted to be like all the other nations. In what areas are you tempted to look to the world around you rather than to God for security and identity?
Samuel's sons repeated the failure of Eli's sons. What does this suggest about the limits of a godly parent's influence and the responsibility of each generation?
God gave the people what they asked for, despite the cost. Can you think of a time when getting what you wanted turned out to be a hard lesson?
